findings.title: Spawned workers are never killed before restart
findings.body: Workers created by multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process are SpawnProcess instances, not instances of the multiprocessing.Process wrapper, so this check is false for production workers. When a worker hangs, the watchdog starts a replacement without killing the original. Repeated stalls accumulate untracked workers beyond max_processes, and a stalled worker that resumes can flush the same shards concurrently with its replacement. The identical check in join() also skips termination. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or explicitly distinguish threads instead.

findings.title: An expired join deadline skips cleanup of remaining workers
findings.body: If next_step.join() or waiting for an earlier worker consumes the timeout, this break exits the loop without terminating any remaining workers. Setting stopped is insufficient for workers blocked in Redis calls or Kafka futures, because they only inspect that flag between flush cycles. Such workers can outlive the strategy and accumulate across rebalances. The deadline should limit waiting, but cleanup must still attempt to terminate every remaining process.

findings.title: The added flusher synchronization sleep is a no-op
findings.body: test_basic replaces time.sleep with a no-op at the start, so this newly added time.sleep(0.1) does not actually wait for the background flusher. poll() does not wait for that worker either, and the following join() sets its stopped flag. Depending on scheduling, the worker can stop before producing the expected message, leaving messages empty and failing the tuple unpack. Synchronize on message production or use an unpatched wait with a bounded timeout.
